about: Eoforwic (York): the Northumbrians' city on the Ouse, its strand at the Foss mouth, minster, book room, mint and halls, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/eoforwic.md, realms/northumbria_york.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified. Woven with the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties run both ways, a story for the spine's thread black_stones is added, beats are pointed at their sites and cards (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json).

ports.summary: The chief city of the Northumbrians: an old stone fortress of the Romans on the Ouse with the archbishop's minster and the best book room north of the Alps inside it, and a trading strand downstream where the Foss runs in. A merchant comes for wool, hides, cloth and jet, and sells wine, quern-stones, pots and, in a hungry year, grain. A Frisian comes carefully: one of his people killed a nobleman's son here twenty years ago, and the dead youth's brother is still counting.
ports.seasons: The way in is the Humber and then the tide up the Ouse, two days of flat banks; the river floods after the winter rains and on the great tides a wave the river men call the Aegir runs up it. Wool comes at midsummer, about Saint Peter's feast (?), hides and salt meat after Martinmas, and from the leaves' fall to Easter the minster and the halls want wine. No fair is recorded: the city buys all year.

history.text: King Edwin was baptised at York at Easter, the twelfth of April, in a wooden church of Saint Peter built for the day. A stone church round it was finished about 637.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.14 (paraphrased); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_York

history.text: About this year Bishop Wilfrid mended Saint Peter's: lead on the roof and glass in the windows.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster; Victoria County History, City of York, 'Before the Norman Conquest'

history.text: The minster burned in April. It burned again in 764.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster; Victoria County History, City of York

history.text: About this year, as the citizens were going out to war, a Frisian merchant killed the son of a count of the province in a brawl, and all the Frisians made haste to leave for fear of the dead youth's kin. Alcuin sent his Frisian pupil Liudger home with them, after three years and six months at the school, with a store of books.
history.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12 (ed. Diekamp 1881; the spine's rendering)

history.text: The church of Holy Wisdom, lofty, with thirty altars, many columns and arches and glazed windows, built for Archbishop Æthelbert by Eanbald and Alcuin, was consecrated ten days before the old man died on the eighth of November. Where it stood is not known.
history.source: Alcuin's poem on the bishops, kings and saints of York, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Æthelbert_of_York

history.text: In Lent a rain of blood fell from a clear sky on the north side of the roof of Saint Peter's, as Alcuin wrote to the king. There was famine in the land, and on the eighth of June heathen men sacked Lindisfarne.
history.source: Alcuin's letter to King Æthelred (MGH Epistolae IV no. 16) (?); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793 (Giles 1847); chronicle_793.json 793-spring-york-blood-rain

history.text: King Æthelred was killed by his own people on the eighteenth of April. Osbald was king twenty-seven days. Eardwulf was consecrated at York on the twenty-sixth of May, at the altar of Saint Paul in the minster. Archbishop Eanbald died on the tenth of August and was buried at York; a second Eanbald, Alcuin's pupil, was consecrated four days later.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 796 (some copies run two years early); Symeon of Durham, Historia regum 796; chronicle_793.json

history.text: Eanbald II received the pallium. About this year Alcuin, now abbot at Tours, asked leave to send boys to York to fetch the books he lacked: 'the flowers of Britain'.
history.source: chronicle_793.json 797-09-08-eanbald-pallium; Alcuin's letter (MGH Epistolae IV no. 121), in G. F. Browne's rendering of 1908 (?)

history.text: Archbishop Eanbald II held a synod at Finchale.
King Eardwulf, driven out about 806, was brought home by the emperor's and the pope's men. Archbishop Eanbald is not heard of afterwards.

From about this year to about 855 the small coin of the Northumbrians, struck at York for kings and archbishops alike, sank from poor silver to plain copper. A bucket buried at Hexham held some eight thousand of them.
Abbot Lupus of Ferrières wrote to Abbot Altsig at York asking for the loan of books: Quintilian, Jerome and Bede.
On the first of November, All Saints' Day, the great army crossed the Humber and took York.
On the twenty-first of March the Northumbrians broke into the city: 'both the kings were slain on the spot. The survivors made peace with the army.' The kings were Osberht and Ælla.
'The army went back to York, and sat there a year.'
The Northumbrians rose against the king the army had set over them; Archbishop Wulfhere fled with him, and came back the next year.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_York; Symeon of Durham, Historia regum 872-873 (?)

history.text: 'Healfden divided the land of the Northumbrians; so that they became afterwards their harrowers and plowers.'
King Guthred, a baptised Dane, died on the twenty-fourth of August and was buried in the minster. About this year the mint, silent for forty years, began to strike good silver pennies.
history.source: Victoria County History, City of York; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_York

history.text: From about this year the empty ground between the fortress and the Foss was laid out in long narrow plots with wattle houses, workshops, pits and wells.
Ragnall, of the kin that held Dublin, took York.
King Athelstan took York and levelled the Danes' stronghold. About then someone buried a gilt Frankish cup with 617 coins in it near Harrogate, and never came back.
history.source: Victoria County History, City of York; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_York_Hoard

history.text: King Athelstan died, and the men of York chose Olaf of Dublin. King Edmund took the city back in 944.

King Eadred burned the minster at Ripon because the Northumbrians had taken Eric for their king. Eric was king twice, and in 954 was driven out and killed on Stainmore. After him earls ruled, and the archbishop Wulfstan, held by the king since 952, was let go.
About this year a monk wrote that York was filled beyond telling with the goods of merchants, who came above all from the Danish people, and that thirty thousand grown people lived there.
history.source: Byrhtferth's Life of Saint Oswald, as given in the Victoria County History, City of York (paraphrased). The number is the monk's, not ours

history.text: Archbishop Wulfstan, who signed himself 'the Wolf', preached his sermon to the English: the world is in haste and nears its end.
Earl Siward died at York and was buried in the church he had built to Saint Olaf at Galmanho, outside the west wall. Tostig, Godwin's son, was made earl.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siward,_Earl_of_Northumbria; Victoria County History, City of York

history.text: On the third of October the thegns of the north rose at York, killed Tostig's men, broke open his treasury and chose Morcar for their earl.

On the twentieth of September the earls were beaten at Fulford by Harald of Norway and Tostig, and York yielded. On the twenty-fifth King Harold came through the city and killed both at Stamford Bridge. Tostig was buried at York. Twenty-four ships were enough to take the Norwegians home.

eras.text: A hungry city with bad omens. Blood ran from the minster roof in Lent, the harvest failed, and on the eighth of June the heathen sacked Lindisfarne; the minster reads Alcuin's letters aloud and collects for the boys carried off. Grain sells for whatever is asked and a Frankish cargo is looked at twice, because King Charles and the English kings have quarrelled over ships. King Æthelred is blamed for all of it, and at Easter 796 his own men kill him.

King Eardwulf and Archbishop Eanbald, Alcuin's pupil, watch each other across the city; the archbishop rides with more spears than a churchman should and shelters the king's enemies. Boys from Tours copy in the book room. The strand by the Foss is busy and the Frisians are still missing from it, unless someone has paid what is owed.

Thirty quiet years under Eanred and then two bad kings at once. No raid, no famine, and the money goes to brass: the moneyers strike small dark coins by the bucket that no stranger will carry home. Bring your own silver and take goods away. The wic by the Foss thins year by year, and by the 850s the mint has stopped.

The army's camp. Both kings are dead inside the wall, the strand is given up, and the archbishop comes and goes as the army allows. Ships in the Ouse belong to the host or pay it. A merchant sells ale, horses and iron to men who weigh their silver, or he stays away.

The army has shared out the land and begun to plough. Danish kings sit at York beside an English archbishop; from about 895 the mint strikes good pennies with Saint Peter's name, and later a sword and a hammer beside it. About 900 the ground between the fortress and the Foss is cut into long plots, and combs, shoes, cups and amber beads are made there. Ships come from the Danes' own country and from Dublin.

Kings by the season. Athelstan pulls down the Danes' stronghold; after him come Olaf, another Olaf, Ragnall, Edmund, Eadred, Eric, Olaf again, Eric again. A safe-conduct dies with the king who gave it, so ask on the Humber who rules before coming up. The town itself grows richer through all of it: silk, amber, soapstone and silver from the far end of the world lie on the benches.

No more kings: an earl for the king of the English, a lawmen's court, and Danish speech in every street. King Edgar lets the Danes keep their own law but every sale needs sworn witnesses, and from 973 the pennies are called in and struck again every few years. York is the second town of England and full of merchants. The raids come back to the south in the 980s and reach the Humber in 993.

Cnut's peace, then Siward's and Tostig's hard hands. Nothing is sold on a Sunday, nothing over four pence without four witnesses, and no Christian is sold out of the land. The earl's house stands at Galmanho outside the west wall beside Saint Olaf's church. In October 1065 the thegns break Tostig's treasury; in September 1066 three hundred Norwegian ships lie in the Ouse, and two battles are fought within a week.

sites.name: The strand at the Foss mouth
sites.see: Boats lie tilted on brown mud where a small river runs into the great one, with posts driven in to tie to and planks laid over the worst of it. Upstream, above the left bank, stands the grey wall of the old fortress with its ten-sided corner tower catching the light. The tide sucks at the bank, men shout the count of bales, and the place smells of river mud, wet wool and tar.
sites.source: The wic at Fishergate where the Foss meets the Ouse (dug 1985-86): en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishergate. No quay is proven; that boats took the ground on the bank is a guess (?). The tower: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_city_walls. No toll rate for 793 is known

sites.name: The wic by the Foss
sites.see: Timber houses stand in rows on the low ground between the two rivers, each with its yard, and goods are sold from the house doors and from boards set on trestles in the lane. In front a woman pours Rhenish wine from a grey jug to be tasted; behind, smoke rises from the bone-workers' and the smiths' sheds. Hammers, a handmill grinding, pigs; the smell of hot horn.
sites.source: Fishergate: eighth and ninth century timber buildings, metal, bone and leather waste; 'the city's principal manufacturing and trading centre', given up in the mid ninth century (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishergate). Rhenish and north French pots and lava querns (?)

sites.name: Wulfheard's yard
sites.see: A long house end-on to the lane, a fenced yard with a storehouse on posts, and a bench under the eaves where the host sits to see who comes up from the strand. Inside, a hearth in the middle, guests' bundles along one wall, and a tally stick for each of them hung on a peg by the door. It smells of malt and of the pig that lives behind the fence.
sites.source: Invented. A stranger traded through a host who answered for him: the Kentish laws of Hlothhere and Eadric 15-16, carried north by the game (?); the spine's hook that a Frisian here 'may trade only through an English host'. From 818 the yard is kept by Wulfheard's heirs

sites.name: Saint Peter's minster
sites.see: A stone church with a roof of dull lead and small windows of real glass that throw coloured light on the floor, somewhere inside the old fortress wall. Edwin's font is here and Saint Paul's altar, where kings are hallowed. Not far off stands a second, taller church, Holy Wisdom, with thirty altars and more columns than a man can count at a glance. Chanting at the hours, a hand-bell, cold stone and beeswax.
sites.source: Wooden church 627, stone 637, Wilfrid's lead and glass about 670, fires 741 and 764, the altar of Saint Paul 796: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster; Victoria County History. Holy Wisdom (Alma Sophia), consecrated 780: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Æthelbert_of_York. Digging in 1967-73 found neither: their places are unknown, and the game does not put them on the present minster

sites.name: The school and the book room
sites.see: A room with a slanted desk under each small window, a scribe at each with a quill and a knife, and along the back wall the chests: more books than a merchant has seen in his life, each chest with a list nailed inside the lid. Boys recite on a bench by the door. Scratching pens, a master's dry voice; the smell of calfskin, oak-gall ink and cold.
sites.source: The school and library, 'probably the largest contemporary collection of books ... outside of Rome' in Wikipedia's words (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Æthelbert_of_York); Alcuin's verses list its authors. Nothing is heard of the library after 866 (Design/content/lore/texts_books.md). Where it stood is unknown

sites.name: The moneyers' bench
sites.see: A lean-to against a stone wall with a block of oak set in the earth floor, an iron die fixed upright in it and a second die in the moneyer's fist. A boy lays a blank, the hammer falls once, and the coin goes into a bowl. In front, a scale no bigger than a hand; behind, a charcoal hearth and a locked chest. It rings like a small bell all day.
sites.source: Stycas for kings and archbishops from the 790s to about 855, pennies again from about 895: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styca; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_York. Two iron coin dies and lead trial pieces from Coppergate (?) (silver_coin.md). The bench stands idle from about 855 to 895

sites.name: The king's hall
sites.see: A long timber hall with a carved door-frame and a porch where spears are left, its thatch dark against the grey Roman stone behind. Inside, a hearth the length of three men, benches along both walls and a high seat with a red cloth on it. Dogs under the boards, a harp on a peg; smoke, roast meat and wet wool.
sites.source: A king's seat at York is certain; where his hall stood in 793 is not known, perhaps inside the fortress (?) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_York). The hall itself is drawn from the common form

sites.name: The kings' garth
sites.see: A fenced court just outside the fortress's east gate, with a hall whose gable beams end in beasts' heads and a row of shields along the wall inside. A king sits here, or after 954 an earl's reeve; a skald stands by the hearth and men throw dice by the door. In the last years the earl keeps his own house instead at Galmanho beyond the west wall, beside Saint Olaf's church.
sites.source: 'Konungsgurtha', the kings' court by the east gate, now King's Square: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_York. Earlsburh at Galmanho and Saint Olave's, built by Siward, who was buried there in 1055: Victoria County History. The four lawmen: Domesday, in the same. The riddle set ymirs_kin (riddles_793.json) is asked here from 905

sites.name: The well in the waste ground
sites.see: Between the fortress and the Foss lies ground nobody has built on since the Romans: nettles, broken tile, elder bushes, and one well, square, lined with oak planks gone black. The water is good and a rope has worn a groove in the kerb. Women come with buckets at dawn and dusk and talk; a heron stands in the wet by the river.
sites.source: Coppergate lay empty after the Romans and was taken up again in the ninth century; a wood-lined well, 1.4 m square, held an eighth-century helmet: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coppergate_Helmet. From about 900 houses stand round it. Offerings at wells are what the later priests' law fines (?)

sites.name: The long plots by the Foss
sites.see: A street of narrow plots running back to the river, each with a wattle house at the street end and a workshop, a pen, a privy and a pit behind. In front a man turns a cup on a pole lathe with his foot; next door a woman saws an antler for comb teeth, and beyond her amber and jet lie half cut on a board. The ground is black and soft underfoot and it stinks.
sites.source: Coppergate, dug 1976-81: four long plots laid out about 900-935, wattle houses and from about 970 cellared plank houses (?), over 40,000 objects, wood, leather and cloth preserved: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorvik_Viking_Centre. The street's name is first written in the twelfth century and its meaning is argued; the game does not use it

sites.name: The building bank below the Foss
sites.see: A stretch of firm bank downstream with a hull on stocks, her strakes held by clamps while a man drives rivets and a boy holds the dolly inside. Split oak lies stacked under a thatch, a pitch pot smokes on three stones, and an old boat lies upside down for her seams. Mallets, an adze chipping, the hiss of a hot iron in tar.
sites.source: Invented: no building place has been dug at York. Clench nails and boat timbers reused in the town are reported from the digs (?); story/ships_793.json names eoforwic as a place where ships are built

sites.name: The ale-house on the old yard
sites.see: A low house with a bush on a pole over the door and a bench outside where three tongues are spoken at once. Inside, a board on trestles, a tub of ale with a dipper, a tafl board scratched on a plank, and a hammer and a cross hung on the same nail by the hearth. Laughter, a dog, dice; malt and smoke.
sites.source: Invented, on the ground of Wulfheard's old yard. Coins of the town carry 'both Thor's hammer and the cross': Victoria County History. Gaming boards and pieces from the York digs (?)

people.name: Wulfheard
people.trait: The host of the strand: slow, fair, curious about every stranger and answerable for them all. His father lodged Frisians, and the yard has been half empty since they ran.
people.want: The Frisians back on the strand with their wine and their short answers, and the old tallies on his wall settled.
people.fear: A guest's knife. A host answers for his guest, and he remembers what the last one cost.
people.voice: Unhurried; asks three questions before he answers one, and remembers every answer next year.
people.looks: Forty-five, broad and soft, thinning fair hair, a brown tunic with a braided hem, a bunch of notched tally sticks at his belt and a horn cup always in reach.
knows: today's prices on the strand, and what the minster cellarer will pay for wine
who was in the brawl of the year the Frisians ran, and who struck first
that Ecgwulf comes down to the strand whenever a Frisian hull is seen
which Frisian tallies still hang on his wall, and whose names are cut on them

ties.note: they were youths together; he will speak to him for a guest, once
her husband Radger left four casks in the storehouse when he fled; Wulfheard sold them and kept the silver aside
remembers a Frisian ship's boy who cried when they cast off
his sister's son, the scribe
sends wine up the coast to the brethren on the Tyne when he has it (?)

Ecgwulf's cousin's widow on the holy island lodges her messengers in his yard, and they bring him the north's news

lines.greet: Whose boat, and who answers for you? Nobody? Then I do, and you sleep under my roof. Three nights makes you my man in law. Try to be dull.
lines.greet_again: My guest again. Your bench is dry and your tally is on the peg. Sit. Tell me what Dorestad pays for wool before you ask about wine.
rumour: It rained blood on the minster in Lent. I saw the stain. A slater says it was rust from the lead. Nobody wants to hear the slater.
The year the Frisians ran I was twenty-five. Thirty hulls gone on one tide. My father stood on the bank and counted what they owed him.
Ecgwulf has seen your sail. He will come down by noon and ask whose she is. Say it plainly. He hates a clever answer.
The king's reeve takes his share of every sale on the strand. He has never told me the same share twice.
lines.feud: A blood-price can be named. It wants the kin, the archbishop's man and silver on a cloak. It has wanted that for twenty years.
lines.saying: A guest is like the tide. Welcome coming in, welcome going out, and you count the posts afterwards.
lines.farewell: Go down on the ebb and tie up at the Trent mouth if the wave is running. Come back. I have told people you will.

people.source: Invented. The name from attested English parts (Wulf-, -heard). The host who answers for a guest of three nights: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric 15 (?). The flight of the Frisians: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11. Thirty hulls is the game's number

people.name: Ecgwulf
people.trait: A Northumbrian thegn whose elder brother was killed by a Frisian merchant in a brawl when Ecgwulf was a youth; patient, correct, and still counting.
people.want: The blood-price, paid before witnesses, or a Frisian of that house within reach.
people.fear: Dying with it unpaid, which would shame his sons.
people.voice: Formal and quiet; names his brother every time he speaks of Frisians.
people.looks: Late thirties, tall, a scar through one eyebrow, long hair and a full beard, a dark red cloak with a silver ring pin, a pattern-welded sword in a worn scabbard.
knows: the name of the ship that fled and of the man who struck: Radger of Dorestad
what a count's son is worth in law, to the penny, and what twenty years add to it
who at the king's hall is rising and who is finished
the roads and halls between York and Bebbanburg

the boy on the ship is a man now

the host of the strand; the one townsman he sits down with

lines.greet: A Frisian hull. Whose is she, and who sails in her? I ask every Frisian. My brother Ecgric would be forty-two this harvest.
lines.greet_again: The same boat. You came back knowing I would be here. That is either honesty or a lack of sense. I have not decided.
rumour: The king blames the bishops and the bishops blame the king, and the heathen have gone home with the boys. I blame slow ships.
At Bebbanburg they saw the sails and stood on the wall. I have told the gate-thegn what I think. He did not disagree.
The archbishop keeps more spears than the king likes. Some of them are mine. Remember that when you choose whom to cheat.
lines.price: Six hundred shillings is the law for a man of his birth. I will hear a number from Radger's house. I will not haggle on the strand.
lines.paid: It is counted. Ecgric's name is said and I have nothing more to ask of your people. It is strange. I thought it would weigh more.
lines.saying: A debt does not sleep. It only lies still so you can step on it.
lines.farewell: Go. Nobody will touch the boat while she lies here. That is not kindness. I want her to come back.

people.source: The spine's cast.ecgwulf (invented). The killing is Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11. The brother's name Ecgric is ours. Six hundred shillings is the game's figure, set between a Northumbrian thegn's and a higher man's worth in the later 'North People's Law' (?)

people.name: Sigewine
people.trait: A Northumbrian monk who carries Alcuin's letters and brings back books: a bad sailor, a good walker, incapable of passing a library.
people.want: A ship that sails when it says it will; a copy of a book York lacks.
people.fear: The sea; arriving with a letter after the man it is for has died.
people.voice: Apologises, then asks for exactly what he needs; complains of the cold like a scribe in a margin.
people.looks: Mid thirties, tall and stooping, tonsured, a patched black cowl, a leather letter case under his arm and a wax-sealed satchel he will not put down.
knows: what Alcuin has written to the king, to Bishop Higbald and to the brethren at Gyrwe
the names of the boys carried off from Lindisfarne, and what the minster has collected for them
which books York has two of and which Tours has none of
every guest-house between the Humber and the Rhine, and its porter's temper

lines.greet: Forgive me. Are you the Frisian with the small boat? I need a passage, a dry corner for this satchel, and a day you will truly sail.
lines.greet_again: You again, thank God, and afloat. I have three letters and a psalter. The psalter does not swim. Neither do I.
rumour: Master Alcuin writes that such terror was never seen in Britain. He writes it to the king, who has seen plenty and caused some.
The minster has collected eleven pounds for the boys the heathen took. Nobody knows where to send it. That is where you come in.
A boy at Gyrwe I taught his letters has gone to sea with a Frisian. If he is yours, make him read. He will pretend he cannot.
lines.letter: This goes to Bishop Higbald, this to Dorestad, this to Tours. If I die at sea, in that order. If you die, I shall be very put out.
lines.saying: My master asks his boys: what is a ship? A wandering house. I have lived in one. The roof is missing.
lines.farewell: God keep you, and keep the wind behind you and the water under you, in that arrangement. I shall be at the book room.

people.source: The spine's cast.sigewine (invented). Alcuin's letters after Lindisfarne: texts_793.json alcuin_793. The riddle of the ship: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini, own rendering of 'Quid est navis? Domus erratica' (?). Eleven pounds is the game's number

people.name: Alcuin
people.trait: The best teacher of his age and a tireless writer of letters: homesick for York's books, fond of riddles and pet names, scolds kings and bishops alike.
people.want: His letters carried and answered; the youths of Lindisfarne ransomed; York's books copied for Tours.
people.fear: That the sack of Saint Cuthbert's church is a judgement on Northumbria's kings, and the beginning of worse.
people.voice: Warm, learned, turns every piece of news into a lesson; met here only as a letter read aloud, for he is over the sea at King Charles's court.
people.looks: Nearing sixty, slight, tonsured grey, a deacon's plain dark dress, ink on his fingers, a pile of wax tablets and a boy to carry them; never seen without a book.
knows: what he has asked King Charles about the boys the heathen carried off
every book in the chests at York, by author
the quarrel of King Charles and King Offa over ships, and how it was mended in 796
riddles for every schoolboy and one for every merchant
