his Frisian pupil, sent home in haste in the year of the brawl
his pupil, whom he scolds as archbishop
who carries his letters
writes to him after the raid
the same bishop, on his island
a priest who heard him teach at York once, forty years ago; now keeper of Saint Oswald's hand on the kings' rock
the abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow, to whom he wrote on his election and again after Lindisfarne: you live by the sea, from which this plague first came
a boy on York's bench in his day, now the best hand at Bede's house; quotes him and resents him
heard him teach at York for one winter and has quoted him ever since; now master of the island's writing house

lines.greet: 'To the merchant who carries this, greeting. You have my thanks and a place in the brethren's prayers. Of silver I say nothing; ask the cellarer.'
lines.greet_again: 'I hear the same Frisian carried my last letter dry across the sea. Tell him a teacher's blessing costs nothing and is worth a little more.'
rumour: 'When I next see the lord king I shall ask about the boys carried off into captivity. Tell their kin I have not forgotten.'
'Send me the flowers of Britain, that the garden may not be shut up in York alone. Copy well. A bad scribe is a slow thief.'
'What use are many spears about an archbishop? Let him be followed by the poor, and he will be safer.'
lines.riddle: 'A boy asks: what is the sea? The road of the bold, the edge of the land, the lodging of rivers. Let the merchant say what a harbour is.'
lines.saying: 'What is a man? A guest of the place, a traveller passing. So pay your host and travel.'
lines.farewell: 'Farewell, and pray for me, who sit among Franks and wine and long for the smell of York's ink.'

people.source: Real. Born York about 735, master from 767, in Northumbria 790-793, abbot of Tours 796, died 19 May 804 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcuin; the spine). He is not at York in person in the game's years. Every line is our own rendering or paraphrase of his letters (MGH Epistolae IV nos. 20, 121, 232 (?)) and of the Disputatio Pippini, never a printed translation

people.name: Eanbald
people.trait: Alcuin's pupil made a lord: keeps more armed men about him than his old master thinks an archbishop should, and shelters the king's enemies.
people.want: Books back from Francia for the minster's library; the upper hand over King Eardwulf.
people.voice: Quick, with schoolroom Latin tags; impatient with merchants unless they carry letters.
people.looks: About forty, vigorous, tonsured, a white woollen band (the pallium) over a rich dark vestment on feast days, a riding cloak and spurs on others, thegns at his back.
knows: what the king said in hall last night, by breakfast
which of the king's enemies are under his roof, and he will not say
what the minster will pay for wine, wax, oil and tin
the law of sanctuary and of blood-price, and how to stand witness to both

ties.note: the same man: this is the spine's Eanbald in his own church
his master, who writes to rebuke his retinue
one of the thegns under his protection
his own scribe, who serves him and the books, in the other order
the island's bishop answers to York and writes very well when he disagrees
the priest of the king's rock is in his province and sends him the hall's news (?)
the abbot of Bede's house: a careful man who asks leave late and humbly; the archbishop wants his books
the abbess of Hild's house asks his leave late and sparingly; he would like her books at York 'for copying'

lines.greet: A merchant. Have you letters? No? Then be brief. Brevitas, as my master never once managed.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who carries letters. Come in out of the wind. You are the only shipman in the province I would give a chair.
rumour: The king put away his wife and took another. I told him so before his thegns. He has not forgiven me, which is how I know he heard.
My master writes that I keep too many spears. My master lives among Franks, where bishops are safe. I answer him politely.
I hallowed a synod at Finchale on the Wear. Good laws, well written. We shall see who keeps them.
lines.witness: A blood-price, before me? Good. Bring the kin, the silver and two men who can count. The Church stands witness and takes nothing. Almost nothing.
lines.saying: Disce ut doceas: learn so you can teach. My master wrote it on every boy. I teach kings. They learn slowly.
lines.farewell: Go with God. If the king's reeve stops your boat, say whose wine is in her. Say it loudly.

people.source: Real: Eanbald II, consecrated 14 August 796, pallium 797, synod at Finchale 798, last heard of 808; sheltered the king's enemies and rebuked his adultery (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eanbald_II; the spine's cast.eanbald). His birth year is a guess (?). The words are ours

people.name: Torhthelm
people.trait: A scribe of the minster with a fine hand and a merchant's eye: he can say what any book cost in calves, years and saints, and to whom it is worth double.
people.want: Good calfskin, red lead, a warm room, and one book in his life that he may copy for love and not by order.
people.fear: Fire in the book room. He was a boy when men still talked of the last one.
people.voice: Dry and exact, with small complaints about his eyes, his fingers and the weather, like notes in a margin.
people.looks: Not yet thirty in 793, short, narrow shoulders, ink-black thumb and forefinger, a grey habit with a penknife and a pumice stone hung from the belt, squinting.
knows: what a book is worth: the herd, the scribe's year, the saint whose it was
which chests hold what, and which book Liudger did not manage to carry away
that boys will come from Tours for the books, and will need a hull
the price of calfskin, wax and pigments in every port a letter has come from

ties.note: his mother's brother, the host on the strand
his lord; he is fond of eating
who brings him exemplars and takes away copies
as a small boy he carried the tall Frisian's ink; he has never forgotten the man's leaving
the island's scribe writes the better hand and both of them know it
they lend each other exemplars up and down the coast and quarrel over their return (?)

lines.greet: Mind the door, the draught turns the page. A merchant? Then you can count. Good. Count the calves in this psalter. One hundred and four.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the dry hold. Sit there, not there, that is the red lead. What have you brought me? Skins? Tell me it is skins.
rumour: Three fingers hold the pen and the whole body aches. Write that down somewhere. No, I have. It is in the margin of Isidore.
Boys are coming from Tours to copy for Master Alcuin. They will want a hull home for a chest. A dry hull. I have named yours.
The heathen tear the covers off for the gold and throw the book in the sea. So a book in the north is cheap, if it floats.
lines.worth: A book is a herd, a year and a saint. Price the herd in a cattle market, the year in a minster, the saint wherever they fear him.
lines.saying: A moth ate words. The thief was no wiser for it. Nor is a man who buys books by weight.
lines.farewell: Go on, I lose the light. If you see good calfskin anywhere between here and the Rhine, think of my eyes.

people.source: Invented; the scribe of the chain cards harbour.chain_lindisfarne_book.s03_calves and end_york. The name is an attested English one (Torht-, -helm). 'Three fingers hold the pen' is the common scribe's colophon, own rendering (?). The moth: Exeter riddle 47, paraphrased (texts_793.json exeter_47_bookworm)

people.name: Wulfhere
people.trait: The archbishop who stayed: he saw the kings killed inside his walls, fled once, came back, and for thirty years kept a church going beside heathen kings by never being quite in the way.
people.want: The minster's lands and its peace left alone, whoever is king; a baptised king if one can be had.
people.fear: That he will be remembered as the army's bishop by the English and as the English bishop by the army.
people.voice: Tired, courteous, exact about what he did and did not promise; speaks of the army as of weather.
people.looks: An old man by 880, thin, a white band over a mended vestment, a plain wooden staff, a heavy ring he turns while he thinks; a Danish boy carries his stool.
knows: which of the army's chief men can be dealt with, and what each takes to be a gift
where the minster's plate went on All Saints' Day, and he will not say
that Saint Cuthbert's people are on the road with the body, and where they rest
who has leave to trade across the line between the two armies

ties.note: the bishop who carries Saint Cuthbert's body about the north; they write when a road is open
baptised her and her Danish father on the same day, and says she was the quieter
a Dane of the first winter's army who now weighs silver honestly in the east (?)
the Frank who cuts Saint Peter's name on the town's pennies in his last year: an honest man, he thinks, for a moneyer
the reeve of the rock beyond the Tyne sends to him for news of the army; he answers with what a bishop may say
the priest who keeps Bede's house on the Tyne; no letter has reached him from there since the army came

lines.greet: You have come up a river full of their ships to sell to my church. Either you are brave or you have leave. Which should I pray for?
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Good. You see we are still here: one bell, nine priests and a roof. I count them each morning.
rumour: On All Saints' Day they came in over the Humber. In Lent our kings came in over the wall and died there. I buried what could be found.
The army has shared out the land and learned to plough. A man with a furrow wants a priest sooner or later, for the weddings.
King Guthred was a slave boy once, bought from a widow. He is baptised and keeps his word. I have known worse kings born to it.
lines.leave: To trade both sides you need a man to stand surety for you. I will stand, once. Do not make a liar of an old man.
lines.saying: They became harrowers and plowers. Write that as the end of a war. It is the truest thing anyone has said of them.
lines.farewell: Go carefully past the ships at the bank. Greet nobody first. And bring wax when you come: we are praying in the dark.

people.source: Real: Wulfhere, archbishop 854 to about 896; fled 872, returned 873 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_York). His birth year is a guess (?). Guthred bought from a widow and made king: Historia de Sancto Cuthberto 13. The id eoforwic.archbishop stands for the seat; after him came Æthelbald, Hrotheweard, Wulfstan I, Oscytel, Oswald, Ealdwulf, Wulfstan II, Ælfric Puttoc, Cynesige and Ealdred, whom the eras name. The words are ours

people.name: Thorgerd
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house on Wulfheard's old yard: daughter of a man of the army and of the host's great-granddaughter, at home in both tongues and cheated in neither.
people.want: Peace long enough to roof the house in oak shingles; her sons on a trading ship and not a raiding one.
people.fear: A new king. Every one of them has wanted the ale free for a month.
people.voice: Quick and loud, Danish when she counts and English when she swears; forgets no face and no debt.
people.looks: A strong woman in her thirties, red hands, fair hair under a linen cloth, a long apron-dress held by two bronze brooches with a string of amber and glass between them, keys and a small hammer and cross on one ring.
knows: who is king this season and who was last, and which of their men drink here
what Dublin ships and Danish ships brought this month, and what they will take home
the old tallies of the yard: she keeps Wulfheard's sticks in the roof, with the names
which lawman can be asked to witness a sale and what he drinks

ties.note: her mother's great-grandfather; the yard and its tallies came down to her
he baptised her; she sends ale to the minster at Easter and asks for nothing
the Frank drinks here and tells her which pennies to refuse
the kings' poet drinks on credit and pays in verses about her ale, none finished
her father's shipmate in the army, who got land at the river mouth under the cliff and sends her jet and eggs

lines.greet: Sit. Ale is a farthing's weight the cup and the first is not free. Where are you from? Say it slowly, I collect accents.
lines.greet_again: I know you. You sat there, drank three and paid for four by mistake. I kept the difference for you. Here.
rumour: There is a new king. Do not learn his name yet. I have stopped until they last a winter.
A Dublin ship came over the hills by the western road, cargo on ponies. Silk, and a man who will not say where he got it.
My father came with the army and stayed for my mother's cooking. He told the priest it was for Christ. The priest had eaten here too.
lines.tally: This stick is older than the Danes in this town. A Frisian name on it. Yours? Then your house has slept on this ground before.
lines.saying: In this town a Frisian, a Dane and an Englishman can all be cheated in each other's tongue. I am the only one who is fair in all three.
lines.farewell: Come back before the leaves fall. I brew strong for Martinmas, and I will have heard everything by then.

people.source: Invented. The name from attested Norse parts (Thor-, -gerd). The mixed town after 876 and the saying: the spine, thread price_of_england, hook for Eoforwic. Hammer and cross together: Victoria County History, of Sihtric's coin. The price of ale is the game's (?)

people.name: Ansbert
people.trait: A Frank who cuts dies and strikes pennies for whichever king holds York: exact, incurious about kings, passionate about silver.
people.want: Clean silver, a steady hand, and a king who lasts long enough to use up one pair of dies.
people.fear: A bad penny traced to his bench. The law for that is a hand, and he needs both.
people.voice: Flat and patient, a Frankish turn to his English; weighs every word as if it might be clipped.
people.looks: Fifty, clean-shaven in the Frankish way, a leather apron scorched at the hem, a short hammer in his belt, forearms like a smith's and spots of burn on both hands.
knows: how much silver is in every penny from the Loire to the Humber, by bite and by colour
which king's name is on the dies this month, and which dies lie ready under the bench
that a great deal of silver went west over the hills and never came back
what the old brass coins of the country are worth now: scrap for the bronze-smith

ties.note: takes the East Anglian's clipped silver without comment and sends him news of new dies (?)
drinks at her house and pays in new pennies, which she tests anyway
the church has a hand in the coin; Saint Peter's name is on it
learned the craft at a Frankish bench on the Seine before the Northmen had it (?)
the Ireland-farer who strikes at Chester for the English king; each bites the other's pennies first
says he was taught by a man taught by a Dorestad moneyer; the house's name opens his chest a little
the kings' poet drinks with him, and agrees that a name lasts longer in silver than in verse; neither is sure

lines.greet: Foreign silver? Put it on the scale, not in my hand. Deniers, dirhams, rings, I do not care. It all becomes Saint Peter in the end.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with honest silver. Rare. I shall take only what the king takes and nothing for myself. Do not tell the others.
rumour: The dies say Cnut on one side and 'he has done wonders' on the other. I asked which wonders. Nobody at the hall could tell me.
They want a sword on the new pennies and a hammer beside the saint's name. I cut what I am paid to cut. Peter also carried a sword once.
A lead box of silver went west toward the Ribble with the Dublin men, more than I strike in three years. It has not been spent. I would know.
lines.brass: These? Old kings' coin of this country. Brass. Eight thousand to the bucket and the bucket was worth more. Give them to a child.
lines.saying: Money has no smell, but silver has a ring. Drop it on the stone and listen before you trust the face.
lines.farewell: Go on. If the king changes before you return, bring those pennies back. I will change them again. At a loss. It is not my law.

people.source: Invented: the 'Frank who strikes for the Danish kings at York' of gipeswic.json. The name from attested Frankish parts (Ans-, -bert). Pennies of Siefred and Cnut from about 895 with MIRABILIA FECIT; Saint Peter pennies about 905-927, some with sword and hammer: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_York; realms/northumbria_york.md (?). Moneyers with Frankish names at York later (Ingalger, Radulf): en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Bloodaxe. The Cuerdale hoard, about 905: silver_coin.md. The Hexham bucket of stycas: the same

people.name: Hallstein
people.trait: The poet of the kings at York: has praised five of them and buried four, keeps the questions of the old giant's kin, and sells them one at a time.
people.want: A king who lives long enough to pay for the second poem; a listener who can answer back.
people.fear: To be the poet of a king nobody remembers. He has the feeling it has happened already.
people.voice: Slow, sidelong, never quite says what he means; names a thing three ways before he names it plainly, and enjoys the wait.
people.looks: Fifty in 925, heavy, a black beard gone grey in two stripes, a blue cloak that was a king's gift and has outlasted him, a silver arm-ring on each arm and a horn he drinks from left-handed.
knows: the line of questions about Ymir's kin, and which hall holds the next one
which king gave which ring, and what each poem cost in nights
that the Dublin poet thinks his own hall the better, and is wrong
what the hall will pay for wine, walrus ivory and a good hawk

ties.note: the poet of the Dublin kings holds the question after his and thinks Dublin the better hall
has heard of an old hall-fellow of Hleidr who went to sea with Frisians; the riddles came north from men like him
the Frank cuts the kings' names; he sings them; they agree the metal lasts longer
three winters of ale, on the strength of a poem about her house he has not finished
the grandson of Ímar who comes from Dublin to be king here in 921; a praise-poem is half made for him, and half paid
an old monk on Columba's island keeps the question after Dublin's; they have never met, and each thinks the other's half the easier

lines.greet: A merchant in a king's hall. Sit low and listen. Or sit higher, if you can tell me what the sky was made of.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who answers. Good. I was tired of asking men who only know the price of things.
rumour: I made a poem for King Ragnall. He paid in a ring. I made one for his heir. He paid in the same ring. Kings are careful here.
The first question is ten pennies' weight: of what was the earth made, and the sky? The rest of the line is not all mine to sell.
The Dublin poet says York is a wet town with a dry hall. He drank here a month before he noticed.
lines.riddle: I have praised the feeder of ravens, the breaker of rings and the reddener of the wolf's tooth. All one man. He owed me for three.
lines.saying: A poem is a debt the king cannot pay in his own coin. That is why they dislike us and keep us.
lines.farewell: Go where the swan's road takes you. That is the sea. I am told merchants prefer it said plainly.

people.source: Invented, to carry the spine's hook (thread price_of_england: York's 'hall sets riddles', riddles_793.json set ymirs_kin, from 905) and the 'poet of the kings at York' of duiblinn.json. The name from attested Norse parts (Hall-, -stein). Skalds were paid in rings: Egil's Head-Ransom (texts_793.json verses). The kennings are the common ones, own wording

people.name: Thored
people.trait: The king's earl at York: a northern man with a Danish name who holds the south of Northumbria for a southern king and trusts neither end of it.
people.want: The Humber kept, his daughter well married, and the house of Bebbanburg kept north of the Tees.
people.fear: A fleet in the Humber in a year when the king's ships are led by fools.
people.voice: Blunt and brief; asks a merchant what he saw at sea before he asks what he sells.
people.looks: Forty, thick-set, a short grey-fair beard, a blue cloak edged with fur and held by a gold ring pin, a sword with a silvered hilt, two hounds at his heel.
knows: what ships have been seen off Spurn and in the Humber this month
King Edgar's law for the Danes: their own customs, and sworn witnesses to every sale
what the house of Bebbanburg holds and wants
when the pennies will next be called in, a little before the moneyers say so

ties.note: the old lord of the rock holds the north of the land and resents the line between them
a young rich man of the town whose ships bring him news
a toll man of the king's on the Thames who writes when a fleet is spoken of (?)
the king's reeve at the water gate on the Dee, where the Dublin road comes down; they trade warnings (?)
his reeve on the staith, who was there before him and expects to be there after

lines.greet: A shipman. Good. What did you see between Spurn and here? Sails, smoke, anything. Then we will talk about your wool.
lines.greet_again: You told me true last time. Sit. I pay for true news in peace on my river, which is worth more than silver.
rumour: The king will have my daughter. It makes me kin to a king and ties me to his luck. I have looked at his luck.
Every sale wants sworn witnesses now. Complain to King Edgar's grave. It has made thieving dear, and that is the only tax I like.
They talk of a fleet gathering at London with bishops to lead it. I am to go. Pray for a ship led by a bishop.
lines.witness: Buy nothing here without two of the sworn men by you. A stranger with an ox and no witness is a thief until the court is tired.
lines.saying: A coast is a long wall with no top. You guard it by knowing first.
lines.farewell: Go down with the ebb. If you meet ships you do not know, do not count them. Come back and tell me you could not.

people.source: Real: Thored, earl at York from about 975 (or 979) to 992; one of the leaders of the king's fleet in 992; his daughter Ælfgifu is held to have married King Æthelred (?) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thored; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 992). His birth year is a guess. Edgar's law for the Danes, 962-963: realms/northumbria_york.md. The id eoforwic.ealdorman stands for the seat: before him Oswulf and Oslac, after him Ælfhelm, Uhtred, Eric of Hlathir, Siward, Tostig and Morcar. The words are ours

people.name: Asketil
people.trait: The king's reeve on the staith since the last king of York was driven out: reads every seal, tag and tally on the river, and has outlived two earls by never having an opinion in hall.
people.want: Every sale witnessed, every bale accounted for, and his son in the office after him.
people.fear: A re-coining. Each one doubles his work and halves his friends.
people.voice: Level and dry; Danish words for goods, English ones for law, and a long pause before either.
people.looks: Fifty, lean, a close grey beard, a brown cloak with a plain silver pin, a tally stick and a bunch of lead tags on a cord at his belt, ink on one thumb.
knows: what came over the hills from the Dee this month, by the lead tags on the cords
which sworn men will stand witness today and which are drunk
the king's share on every kind of sale, and the earl's, and the archbishop's in his own shire
when the old pennies stop being money

ties.note: his fellow at Chester, whose lead tags he reads at this end of the hill road
the earl of the day; Thored is his third
a young man with too many shares in too many ships, all of them correctly witnessed, which is what worries him
was a boy on the staith when Amlaíb was king in York, and is careful never to say so

lines.greet: Tie up there. What is in her, who sold it to you, and who saw him do it? Take your time. I have until the tide.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. Your witnesses were good last time. I checked. I always check. Do not take it to heart.
rumour: A bale came over the hills with a Chester tag on its cord. Goods under that seal I do not ask about twice. Once, I ask.
King Edgar has called in every penny in the land. New ones, one face, forty towns. Yours go to the bench at the moneyer's price.
The Danes here keep their own law, by the king's leave. I am a Dane. I still want four men who saw you buy that horse.
lines.sunday: Nothing is sold, loaded or carted on the Lord's day. I did not make the law. I only enjoy the quiet.
lines.saying: A thief and an honest man carry the same sack. The difference is who watched him fill it.
lines.farewell: Go on the ebb. Your tally is square. That is the kindest thing I say to anybody.

people.source: Invented: the 'fellow at York' of legacaestir.json's reeve Beorhtwine. The name from attested Norse parts (As-, -ketil). The king's reeve and the city's shires: Domesday, by way of the Victoria County History. Edgar's law for the Danes with sworn witnesses to every sale (962-963) and the re-coining of 973: realms/northumbria_york.md; chronicle_793.json 973-edgar-coinage. The Sunday rule is written down only about 1020 (?)

people.name: Styr
people.trait: Styr, Ulf's son: the richest man in York, with ships, plots and a long feud with Thurbrand the hold; gives land to Saint Cuthbert and a daughter to an earl, both on terms.
people.want: Thurbrand dead. He made it a condition of his daughter's marriage, in so many words.
people.fear: That his son-in-law the earl will prefer a new king's favour to an old father's bargain.
people.voice: Pleasant, slow, generous at table; states his terms once and never repeats them.
people.looks: A big man past fifty, white-fair beard combed and forked, a red tunic with silk at the cuffs, a silver arm-ring on each wrist, and a walking staff with a walrus-ivory head.
knows: what every ship on the staith carries and who has a share in her
the feud of Uhtred's house and Thurbrand's, which will outlive them both
which plots by the Foss are for sale and what the earl's reeve takes on them
what Dublin, the Danes' country and the Rhine pay for York's goods this year

ties.note: his daughter Sige's husband: given on the promise that Uhtred would kill Thurbrand
the earls of York dine at his board; he has outlasted three
his brother's granddaughter, who has the old ale-house and one of his ships
the king at Dublin, whose new pennies copy the English king's; Styr's ships carry them over the hills (?)
bowed with the rest of the north in 1016, and counted what it cost
a shipmaster of the western isles with whom he trades marten skins and old questions

lines.greet: A Frisian house, and an old one, they tell me. Eat first. I never talk shares with a hungry man. He agrees too quickly.
lines.greet_again: My friend from over the sea. Your goods sold well when you had gone. I took my part and here is yours, counted before two sworn men.
rumour: I gave my daughter to Earl Uhtred with one condition. He knows it. Thurbrand knows it. So everybody sleeps lightly.
King Æthelred sat in this town and I gave Saint Cuthbert good land before his eyes. A saint keeps a gift longer than a king.
The town is so full of merchants a man cannot spit. Most are Danes. The rest are learning to be.
lines.share: A third of a ship is better than a whole one. When she sinks you weep a third. When she comes home you have two friends.
lines.saying: A gift looks for a gift. I look a little harder than most.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you hear Thurbrand's name on any quay, remember who fed you.

people.source: Real: Styr son of Ulf, a rich man of York, who gave his daughter Sige to Uhtred on condition that he kill Thurbrand (De obsessione Dunelmi, Stevenson 1855), and gave land to Saint Cuthbert when King Æthelred was at York (Historia de Sancto Cuthberto 29 (?)). His years are guesses round those two facts. That he owned ships is the game's. 'A gift looks for a gift' turns Hávamál 46 (Bellows 1923)

people.name: Gunnulf
people.trait: The wright of the building bank: fourth of his line on that mud, builds by eye and by his grandfather's rods, and distrusts any ship he did not hear being built.
people.want: Seasoned oak knees, good iron, and an order for one great ship before his hands go.
people.fear: The earls' wars. Every one has ended with his best hull pressed and never paid for.
people.voice: Few words, most of them about wood; answers a price with a silence and then a lower one.
people.looks: Forty in 1040, short and wide, a brown beard with pitch in it, a leather apron, a tunic out at the elbows, an adze over one shoulder and a rivet-counter's pouch at his belt.
knows: what any hull on the river is worth, by the sound of a knuckle on her strakes
where oak for a keel can still be had in the Vale, and who owns it
which ships the earl has pressed and which are hidden
what the Dublin yard is building, by word of mouth through skippers

ties.note: the master of the Dublin yard: iron goes west and seasoned knees come east, and neither has seen the other's face
built the ship she has a third of, and knows where it is under the hay
as a young man he built for Styr, who paid on the day, which he has never forgotten
the reeve under the cliff sends him wrecked timber worth saving

lines.greet: That your boat? Hm. Danish-built, a long time ago, and mended by Frisians. Badly. Well. Not badly. Differently.
lines.greet_again: She still floats. I knocked on her when you were at the ale-house. Third strake, starboard. Bring her up before the frost.
rumour: The Dublin yard has laid a keel for sixty oars. Sixty. I sent iron for her. I would give a finger to hear her launched.
Earl Tostig's men counted the hulls on my bank. A man who counts your ships is not going to pay for them.
Oak is going. My grandfather cut keels a morning's walk from here. I send to the Derwent now, and pay a monk for the leave.
lines.price: A winter, forty oaks, and silver down for the iron. I will not say a day. The wood says the day.
lines.saying: A ship is never finished. You only stop and push her in.
lines.farewell: Go easy on her in the Humber chop. And come back by my bank, not the other one. He uses green wood.

people.source: Invented: the 'wright on the Ouse' of duiblinn.json's Asgrimr. The name from attested Norse parts (Gunn-, -ulf). The great ship built at Dublin in these years is real (Skuldelev 2, of Irish oak felled about 1042 (?)); the trade in iron and knees is the game's. No building place has been dug at York (?)

people.name: Sigrid
people.trait: A widow of the town with the old ale-house, a plot by the Foss and a third of a ship: of Wulfheard's and Thorgerd's line, and the keeper of their tally sticks.
people.want: Her son home from the earl's following alive, and the house kept out of the earls' quarrels.
people.fear: Earl Tostig's tax men; and after 1065, whoever comes to answer for them.
people.voice: Calm and wry; speaks English with Danish words for every tool and every insult.
people.looks: Fifty in the last years, straight-backed, grey hair under a silk-edged cap, a dark gown with a round silver brooch, a ring of keys and a pair of folding scales at her belt.
knows: what Earl Tostig took in tax this year and from whom
who among the thegns has stopped coming to the earl's hall
the price of everything on the staith, in pennies of the newest issue
the oldest stick in her roof, with a Frisian name cut on it, and the story that goes with it

ties.note: her father's mother's mother; the house, the keys and the tallies came down the women
her grandfather's brother, from whom she has her share in a ship
a priest of Saint Cuthbert's who lodges with her when he brings letters to the archbishop
the earl's reeve under the cliff, through whom she buys raw jet for the cutters on her plot
built the ship she has a third of; she pays him in ale, and he tells nobody where the hull is hidden

lines.greet: A Frisian. Wait. There is a stick in my roof with a Frisian name on it, older than the Danes here. Tell me yours.
lines.greet_again: The house of the old stick. Come in. Your people have had a bench here for nine lifetimes. I will not be the one to move it.
rumour: Earl Siward asked for his mail and his axe to die in. He said he would not die lying down like a cow. He did it standing.
Earl Tostig hangs robbers, which is good, and then taxes as if we were the robbers. My neighbour has stopped going to hall.
Three hundred ships lie at Riccall, they say. My third of a ship is hidden up the Foss under hay. Do not look at me like that.
lines.rising: They broke the earl's treasury on the third day of the tenth month and took back the tax. I got eleven pennies. I am told that is justice.
lines.saying: Earls come like weather. Shut the door, mind the fire, count the hens after.
lines.farewell: Go while the river is yours. If it goes badly here, there is a bench at my fire and a roof with your name in it.

people.source: Invented. The name from attested Norse parts (Sig-, -rid). Siward's death 'like a cow': Henry of Huntingdon, twelfth century, paraphrased (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siward,_Earl_of_Northumbria). The rising of 3 October 1065 and the treasury: John of Worcester (?). Riccall and the three hundred ships: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1066

stories.title: The year the Frisians ran
stories.summary: About 773 a Frisian merchant killed a count's son here and every Frisian fled on one tide; the blood-price was never paid. The dead youth's brother Ecgwulf comes down to the strand whenever a Frisian hull is seen, and the richest market of the north stays half shut to the house until somebody counts silver onto a cloak before the archbishop.
stories.picture: A grey morning on a muddy river strand: a tall thegn in a dark red cloak stands with his hand on his sword hilt looking down at a small Frisian boat; in her stern a man sits with his hood up and his back turned; the fortress wall behind.

beats.text: A Frisian hull is looked at twice. Ecgwulf comes down by noon and asks whose she is and who sails in her. Answer truly and he knows the house (sets yk_named); she may trade only through an English host.

Wulfheard answers for his guest and tells the story as he saw it at twenty-five: the muster, the brawl, thirty hulls gone on one tide (sets yk_feud_known). He shows a tally stick with Radger's name on it and four casks' worth of silver he has kept aside for twenty years.
The widow Thiadburg hears that Ecgwulf lives and will hear a number. She asks what it weighs, and puts a third of it on the table.
Aldger's kin say what the boy saw from the ship in 773: who drew first. It does not change the price. It changes how it can be asked.

beats.when: year < 813 and flag.yk_named and not flag.yk_price_set
beats.text: In hall, before his lord, Ecgwulf names his brother and the law's figure. He will take silver, or goods he chooses, or a service.

beats.when: year >= 796 and year < 809 and flag.yk_named and not flag.yk_price_set
beats.text: Archbishop Eanbald stands witness himself: the price is named before him and written down (sets yk_price_set). Before 796 his clerk does it, with less Latin.

beats.when: year < 813 and flag.yk_price_set and not flag.yk_paid
beats.text: Ecgwulf, at the king's rock for a feast, names the service he would take in place of half the silver: wine and Frankish blades carried to his lord through a hungry year.

beats.when: year < 813 and flag.yk_price_set and not flag.yk_paid
beats.text: The kin stand in a half circle on the strand, a cloak is spread, and the silver is counted onto it before the archbishop's man and two who can count (sets yk_paid). Ecgric's name is said aloud once.
The next morning the steersman Aldger walks the strand under his own name, slowly, the whole length of it, and Wulfheard walks beside him.

beats.when: year < 813 and flag.yk_price_set and not flag.yk_paid
beats.text: Without a marriage the price is counted out all the same: three pounds by weight, or the two pounds the scribe's letter left, or half and the errand named on the rock.
Wulfheard lifts his hearthstone and counts out the pound he has kept for Radger's four casks, and breaks the stick with the black notch.

beats.when: year < 813 and flag.yk_named and not flag.yk_paid
beats.text: On the holy island the widow Æthelgyth, a cousin by marriage of Ecgwulf's house, will send word to York for a merchant who has carried for the boys. He listens to her about one time in three.
A scribe at Bede's house was a boy on the bank that day, and saw who drew first. His letter to the archbishop's clerk is worth a third of the price.

endings.how: The merchant gathered the price, with or without the widow's third, and counted it out on the strand before witnesses.
endings.text: Ecgwulf says he thought it would weigh more, and never mentions Frisians again. Within two summers there are Frisian hulls at the Foss mouth, and they ask for the house by name.
endings.reward: Sets yk_paid: Eoforwic opens to the house and to Frisians; no host is needed; Ecgwulf friendly for life and his sons at half strength; Wulfheard pays over Radger's kept silver, about 240 d; Thiadburg stands surety for the count's debt (db_surety); Aldger's heart mended

endings.how: The merchant took Ecgwulf's errand: wine, grain and blades for his lord, carried through the hungry years at the merchant's own risk.
endings.text: The price is called paid at half its weight. Ecgwulf treats the house as his lord's men, which is closer than friendship and has more duties.
endings.reward: Sets yk_paid at half the silver; a standing commission from Ecgwulf's lord for wine and iron; a seat on the bench at Bebbanburg; the king's men on the Frankish side may hear of the blades (sw_marked is possible)

endings.how: The merchant's heir asked for the dead youth's daughter, and the price became a bride-gift (the chain house_marriage, the English road).
endings.text: The feud ends in a wedding on the strand. The house has English kin at York, and a great many of them come to dinner.
endings.reward: Sets yk_paid; an English marriage for the house; guest-friendship at Eoforwic for the heirs (flag guest_friend_eoforwic); Ecgwulf's kin answer for the house in any Northumbrian court

endings.how: Nothing was paid before Ecgwulf died, about 812.
endings.text: His sons inherit the count and none of his patience. A Frisian hull is turned off the strand for a generation; the house trades at Eoforwic only through Wulfheard's heirs and at their price, until the army comes in 866 and the old feud is nobody's business.
endings.reward: Nothing. Prices a tenth worse at Eoforwic until 866; Aldger never goes ashore here; Thiadburg's good will lost

stories.reward: The richest market of the north opened to the house and to its people, a thegn's friendship, the steersman's peace, and the widow's backing at home.

stories.title: The flowers of Britain
stories.summary: About 797 Alcuin, abbot at Tours, sends boys to York to copy the books he lacks. They need a dry hull home for a chest worth more than the ship, and a scribe at York will teach a merchant what a book is worth and to whom.
stories.picture: A book room with small bright windows: two boys in travelling cloaks packing books into an iron-bound chest lined with waxed cloth, a squinting scribe checking each against a list, a merchant in a short Frisian cloak measuring the chest with a knotted cord.

beats.text: Torhthelm prices any book a merchant can describe: the herd, the scribe's year, the saint (sets bk_knows_worth).

beats.when: year >= 797 and year < 804 and not flag.bk_carried
beats.text: Two boys from Tours have copied all winter. The chest is packed and listed, and Sigewine has named the merchant's hull as a dry one. The archbishop wants surety; the scribe wants the chest kept off the bilge.

beats.when: year >= 797 and year < 804 and not flag.bk_carried
beats.text: Eanbald will let the copies go and not one exemplar. He counts the books out himself, and one too few goes into the chest. Torhthelm coughs. The archbishop puts it back.
At the toll of Quentovic books are not goods, says Abbot Gervold's clerk, unless they are sold. The chest passes free on Alcuin's name; a merchant who tries to sell a leaf pays for the whole.
At the Loire mouth men of Saint Martin's wait with a river boat to take the chest up to Tours. They pay as abbeys pay: some silver, a letter, and a standing order (sets bk_carried).
The schoolmaster of Saint Martin's at Traiectum has heard. He opens the chest of books Liudger brought from York in the year of the brawl, and asks what York would send now (sets bk_parchment).
A letter has come from an abbot in Francia asking for the loan of Quintilian, Jerome and Bede. The book room is slower now and colder. It is the last such letter anyone here remembers.

The coast's writing houses reckon a book alike and lend each other the exemplars: at Bede's house Torhtred does the same sum for the master's history, and on the island Ceolhelm for a gospel book without its lid.

endings.how: The chest reached the Loire mouth whole and dry.
endings.text: Alcuin writes a letter of thanks that is read aloud at York, Tours and Traiectum, and for a generation monks in three realms know the name of a Frisian house.
endings.reward: Sets bk_carried; about 400 d from Saint Martin's; Alcuin's letter (give_text alcuin_793 if not held); standing with every church the letter is read in; a yearly order for calfskin and pigments at Eoforwic (bk_parchment)

endings.how: The chest was lost to water or thieves on the way.
endings.text: Two boys go home with nothing and a winter of work is at the bottom of the sea. Torhthelm does not speak of it; he begins again, and asks for another hull.
endings.reward: Sets bk_lost; the surety is forfeit (about 300 d); the book room cool to the house for five years; nothing else: nobody thinks a merchant can command the sea

endings.how: The merchant had a second copy made on the quiet and sold it in another port.
endings.text: A Frankish abbey has a book it should not, and is very pleased. Torhthelm recognises his own hand in it some years later, in a letter's description, and says nothing to his lord.
endings.reward: About 600 d from the buyer; bk_knows_worth; Torhthelm cool for good, though he keeps the secret; if the archbishop learns of it the minster's custom is lost

stories.reward: A trade no rival understands: what a book is worth and to whom, a standing order from a scriptorium, and a name read aloud in churches.

stories.title: Blood on the roof
stories.summary: In Lent of 793 blood rained from a clear sky on the north side of Saint Peter's roof; the harvest failed and the heathen came to Lindisfarne. A cargo of grain is worth a king's thanks that year, the minster is collecting to ransom the boys carried off, and a priest has a letter that must reach Dorestad.
stories.picture: A stone church with a grey lead roof under a clear cold sky, a dark red stain running down the north slope to the eaves; below, thin people queue at a door where a monk measures grain from a merchant's sack with a wooden bowl.

beats.text: The stain is still on the lead. A priest says it came from the north, where the blood would come from; a slater says rust. The minster reads Alcuin's letter to the king aloud, and people weep, and the king's men do not.
Bread is a third bark. Grain from over the sea sells at once, at any price the seller has the face to ask. The minster's almoner stands at the back and watches what he asks.

The king has heard who sold grain and at what price. A fair seller is thanked before the benches and given the king's word on the strand; a dear one is asked, pleasantly, to stay for the reeve's counting.

Sigewine has the names of the boys taken from Lindisfarne and the sum the minster has collected. Nobody knows where to send it. He gives the merchant the names and a letter for the priest at Dorestad (sets lf_knows_boys).
The priest on the dam has a letter from York, thirteen days behind the news it carries. He wants a book taken to Traiectum, and word sent back.
Bishop Higbald hears what York has collected and says what he will add. He does not think the boys are alive. He would like to be wrong.
Word that a boy lives is brought to York. The collected silver, eleven pounds, is counted out to the merchant before the altar of Saint Paul, with a list of witnesses as long as his arm.
At Bede's house the cellarer will take barley at a price he can say aloud in chapter, and gives a fair seller the old abbot's riddle of the fish.
On the island the cellarer's own farm has sent excuses in place of corn. Two sacks of barley left at the half door are remembered longer than silver.

endings.how: The merchant sold grain at or under the fair price and carried the names and the silver north.
endings.text: The minster writes the house into its book of the living. When a boy comes home, the bell of Saint Peter's is rung for a merchant's ship, which nobody remembers happening before.
endings.reward: Sets hy_fed_poor and lf_knows_boys; the king's thanks (no toll on the strand until Æthelred's death in 796); the minster's custom in wine and wax; 2640 d of ransom silver in trust, and a tenth of it in thanks if a boy is brought home

endings.how: The merchant sold grain for what the famine would bear.
endings.text: He leaves with a full purse and a quiet strand. The almoner has a long memory, and the reeve counts the next cargo to the last grain.
endings.reward: Sets hy_sold_dear; half as much again on the grain, about 300 d on a full boat; the minster cool; the reeve searches the boat each time for three years

endings.how: The merchant took the ransom silver in trust and did not carry it north.
endings.text: Nobody at York learns of it for some years. Then Sigewine does, and writes one letter, to every church the house trades with.
endings.reward: 2640 d; shunned by the churches of Northumbria, Frisia and the Loire once the letter is read; Beornwine leaves the crew

stories.reward: A king's thanks, the minster's custom and its prayers, and the names that open the trail of the boys of Lindisfarne.

stories.title: A bucket of brass
stories.summary: From the 830s the York moneyers strike small dark coins by the thousand that hold almost no silver, and a buyer here pays in them by the bucket. Nobody over the sea will take one. A merchant must learn to take goods, test silver, or find the one use brass has.
stories.picture: A wooden bucket brim-full of small dark coins on a trestle in a market lane, a York buyer pushing it across with one finger and a Frisian merchant looking into it as into a well; a boy behind bites a coin and pulls a face.

beats.text: A buyer offers a fair price for wine, in stycas: eight thousand to the bucket. It is the king's coin and to refuse it is an insult. To take it is worse.

The moneyer of the day, a man who cuts handsome dies for ugly metal, says plainly what is in them: brass, tin, a memory of silver. He will change them for goods, never for silver (sets sv_scale if the merchant buys a scale from him).
The moneyer at Dorestad looks at a York coin, laughs, and drops it in the scrap. Then he says what a bronze-smith would give for a bucket of them by weight.
The host's heirs keep two tallies now: one in the king's coin for the reeve's eyes, and one in fleeces and hides, which is the true one.
Ansbert the Frank finds an old styca in a merchant's purse and holds it up to the boy at the bench as a lesson. Then he strikes a good penny on the same block.
At Hild's house on the cliff the cellarer is paid in the king's brass by the bucket, and the cliff men keep their best jet for the buyer who brings iron and salt.

endings.how: The merchant refused the bucket politely and took fleeces, hides and jet at the tally price.
endings.text: The buyer shrugs: every stranger says the same. The house learns to come to York with silver of its own and leave with a full hold, and does well out of thirty quiet years.
endings.reward: Wool, hides and jet at a tenth under the strand price while the stycas last; the host's true tally opened to the house

endings.how: The merchant took the bucket cheap and carried it to a bronze-smith over the sea.
endings.text: It is heavy, it is ugly, and at Dorestad or Ribe it is good casting metal for brooches. Nobody has ever made less on eight thousand coins, or lost nothing on them.
endings.reward: About 60 d of profit on a bucket and the tip rw_tip_eoforwic; a bronze-smith's friendship in the port where it is sold; the moneyer at York amused

endings.how: The merchant said aloud in the market what the king's coin was worth.
endings.text: He was right, and the reeve fines him for it, in silver.
endings.reward: A fine of 40 d in real silver; the strand cool for a season; the moneyer buys him a drink in private

stories.reward: The habit of weighing and testing every coin, a true price for York's goods in the brass years, and a moneyer's respect.

stories.title: All Saints' Day
stories.summary: On the first of November 866 the great army comes over the Humber and takes York; in Lent both kings die inside the wall. The town that grows out of it has Danish kings, an English archbishop and a market for everything, and it ends two hundred years later with three hundred Norwegian ships in the Ouse.
stories.picture: A feast-day morning turned wrong: riders on small horses pouring through a gap in a grey Roman wall, smoke from thatch, a priest hurrying with a bundle under his cloak; in front, a merchant on the river bank with one hand on his mooring rope.

beats.text: The merchant lies at the strand for the feast when the army rides in. Leave on the tide, hide the silver, or sell ale and iron to the new masters: each is remembered.
The same army wintered in East Anglia and rides East Anglian horses. A York man asks where the merchant was in the winter of the horses.
Wulfhere has buried two kings and what could be found of their men. The plate is gone from the altars; he does not say where. He asks for wax, and whether any road is open to Saint Cuthbert's people.

Thorgerd's house on the old yard. To trade both sides of the line between the armies a man needs a surety; she names the lawman to ask and the archbishop will stand for him, once (sets en_hostage_given).

In the kings' hall a skald sets riddles of the old giant's kin for silver, and a merchant who answers is seated higher. In Eric's day a tale goes round of an Icelander who made a praise-poem in one night to buy back his own head.
The kings of York and of Dublin are one kin, and their road runs over the hills. A Dublin skipper asks who is king at York this season, and offers half a cargo to a man who can say truly.
King Athelstan has pulled down the Danes' stronghold. Pennies with the sword and the hammer must go to the bench and come back fewer, with the king's name on them.
Earl Thored pays for true news of sails with peace on his river. He is called to the king's fleet in 992, and the merchant who warned him of its leaders is remembered or not, as it falls out.

Three hundred ships lie at Riccall. Sigrid has hidden her share of a ship up the Foss under hay. King Harald of Norway wants hulls, the earls want hulls, and in five days King Harold of the English will want to know who gave them.

endings.how: The merchant sold to the army in 866 and kept coming.
endings.text: The house is known at York as the Frisians who never left. It has a plot by the Foss by 900 and kin in two tongues, and south of the Humber it is asked, now and then, whose side it was on.
endings.reward: A plot at Eoforwic at half price (unlock_plot_eoforwic); en_followed_silver; friendly with the Danish kings' men; cool with the English reeves of the south until 927

endings.how: The merchant carried wax, letters and the archbishop's people through the army's years.
endings.text: Wulfhere stands surety for the house and writes its name where the minster keeps the names of its friends. Every later archbishop reads it there.
endings.reward: Sets en_hostage_given without cost; the minster's custom to 1066; sanctuary and lodging at Saint Peter's for the heirs; bk_carried if a book went with the letters

endings.how: The merchant left on the tide and did not come back until the pennies were good again, about 895.
endings.text: He lost thirty years of the town and none of his silver. The ale-house on the old yard still has the stick with his house's name, and Thorgerd makes him pay for the first cup.
endings.reward: Nothing lost; no standing at Eoforwic before 895; the tally stick, and with it the old host's line as friends from the first visit

endings.how: In September 1066 the merchant gave his hull to one side: Harald of Norway's, the earls', or neither.
endings.text: The Norwegians pay in promises and go home in twenty-four ships. The earls lose on the twentieth and are forgiven on the twenty-fifth. A hull hidden up the Foss is still a hull when it is over.
endings.reward: With the earls: King Harold's thanks, briefly worth a great deal. With Norway: 300 d in hand and the ship lost. Hidden: the ship, and Sigrid's bench for the house's last winter in the game

stories.reward: A place in the town that comes after: a plot, a surety, kin in two tongues, and the choice of where the house's hull lies in the last September.

stories.title: A line about merchants
stories.summary: Alcuin was at York from 790 to 793 and wrote from Northumbria of the quarrel between King Charles and King Offa, which shut each king's shores to the other's merchants. The minster's scribes know his letters. One sentence of one of them, copied fair, is the nearest thing to law that a Frisian with English goods aboard can carry; whether Northumbrian ships were barred too, nobody here can say (?).
stories.picture: A cold room of slanted desks and book chests: a short scribe with an ink-black thumb holds a letter up to a small window and points at one line with his penknife, while a Frisian merchant in a short cloak leans in to look.

beats.text: The scribe Torhthelm reads out Alcuin's line: on both sides the passage of ships is forbidden to merchants. He does not know whether Northumbrian ships are meant, and says that scholars never write down the one thing a shipman needs.
The minster's cellarer has had little Rhine wine for three summers, and will pay well over the strand's price for what a Frisian keel brings through the quarrel.
On King Offa's far shore the lead man has the line read to him twice: forbidden to English merchants. A Frisian hull is not an English one. It is worth a penny a pig.
At the abbot's own toll the same sentence is either a friend's errand or a broken ban, according to who is on the bank that day.

A later letter comes north: the kings are friends again, true pilgrims go free, traders pay the toll, and black stones are to be cut to the length the English ask. The scribe files it beside the first, and says the pair would make a short book about kings.

endings.how: The merchant paid for a fair copy of the line and carried it to the Dee.
endings.text: The lead man cannot read it, and believes it the more for that. A sentence written at York by a scribe who has never seen the sea moves six pigs of lead across it.
endings.reward: Lead at nine pence the pig from Beornoth while the ban stands (the card harbour.forty_pigs.legacaestir); a little Latin; the scribe's goodwill

endings.how: The merchant took the cellarer's order and brought Rhine wine through the quarrel.
endings.text: The altar and the high table have their wine by a Frisian keel, and the cellarer asks no questions about how it passed whose toll.
endings.reward: Three casks at a third over the strand's price (a commission); the minster's custom after

endings.how: The merchant heard the line read and left it in the book.
endings.text: He knows now why English cloth is dear at Dorestad and quernstones lie unsold there, which is more than most skippers know.
endings.reward: Nothing but the knowledge

stories.reward: A sentence of Alcuin's in the merchant's keeping, cheaper lead on the Dee while the kings quarrel, and the minster's wine custom.

works.name: Tin for the minster's bell-house
works.what: The minster is roofing its little bell-house and wants tin for it and wine for the men, as Alcuin himself once sent from Francia. The merchant pays for the metal and brings it; the church does the rest.
works.picture: A small square timber tower beside a stone church, two men on its roof laying bright sheets of tin, a bell hanging in the open frame below and a cask of wine being rolled up to the door.
works.needs: tin brought from the south or from Francia; the archbishop or his clerk on easy terms
works.gives: The bell is rung for the house's ship coming up the river in fog; alms and vows at the minster count double for standing; the archbishop will stand witness for the house without a gift
works.source: Alcuin sent wine and tin from Francia for the minster's bell-house: Victoria County History, City of York; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eanbald_II. The price is the game's

works.name: A storehouse on posts in the host's yard
works.what: A plank store raised on posts above the flood, with a door that locks and a tally of its own, built in a corner of Wulfheard's yard by his leave.
works.picture: A small plank building on six stout posts in a fenced yard, a ladder to its door, casks and bales being handed up, brown flood water standing in the lane outside.
works.needs: Wulfheard or his heirs friendly; before 813, the blood-price paid or a host's surety
works.gives: Goods kept dry and safe at Eoforwic between voyages (store without rent); the host sells from it for the house at a twentieth; the floods do not reach it
works.source: Invented. Timber buildings in the Fishergate wic: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishergate. The Ouse floods: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Ouse,_Yorkshire. Agrees with story/unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_eoforwic

works.name: A book copied for the house
works.what: Torhthelm, or the scribe after him, copies a psalter or a gospel in the book room for the merchant to give where he chooses: a year of a man's life, a hundred calves, red and yellow in the capitals.
works.picture: A scribe at a slanted desk by a small window, the last leaf of a book under his pen, a stack of finished gatherings tied with cord beside him and a merchant counting silver onto the sill.
works.needs: the scribe friendly; calfskin and pigments brought by the merchant, or a third more silver
works.gives: A book to give: to a church for standing in a whole region, or to a king's hall as a gift nobody else can make; the book room's custom in skins and colours
works.source: Invented. The scale of the work from the Lindisfarne dossier (some 150 calfskins for the great gospels); the York school and library: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Æthelbert_of_York. The price is the game's

works.name: A length of staith on the Foss bank
works.what: Oak piles and a wattle face along the muddy bank behind a plot, backfilled with brushwood and earth, so that a loaded hull can lie afloat at half tide beside her own door.
works.picture: Men knee-deep in mud driving oak piles with a great wooden beetle, woven wattle between the piles, a trading ship waiting in the stream and a narrow plot with a wattle house running back from the bank.
works.needs: a plot by the Foss; the lawmen's leave (a gift to the hall)
works.gives: Loading and unloading at Eoforwic in half the time and without porters; a larger ship can lie here; the plot's worth rises by half
works.source: Invented. The long plots running back to the Foss from about 900: the Coppergate dig. Timber river fronts are known at other towns of the time; none is proven at York in these years (?)

works.name: A carved stone in the minster yard
works.what: A grave slab of local stone for one of the house who died here, cut by a York carver with a cross down its length and beasts in the Danish manner biting their own tails along the edges.
works.picture: A long flat stone in a crowded graveyard under a church wall, freshly cut: a cross, a knot of ribbon-bodied beasts, a carver brushing dust from it and a widow with keys at her belt watching.
works.needs: one of the house or its crew buried at Eoforwic; alms given at the minster
works.gives: The dead of the house are remembered here by name at every All Saints; the heirs begin with the town's good will; the crew's heart is steadier in the north
works.source: A graveyard with carved slabs of the tenth and eleventh centuries lay under the later south transept of the minster (?): the dossier, from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster. Danes buried in churchyards under carved stones within two generations (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter on the bank below the Foss, or bought second-hand from a York house
ships.note: Oak from the Vale and a market that fills a deep hull: wool and hides out, wine and quern-stones in. Until the blood-price is paid no York wright will lay a keel for a Frisian without an English name on the order.
ships.picture: A beamy clinker hull on stocks on a muddy river bank, half planked, split oak stacked beside her, the grey fortress wall far behind.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json names eoforwic among the places she is built. No building place has been dug at York (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand from the minster or one of its daughter houses, when the cellarer parts with an old one
ships.note: The archbishop's church has lands and cells down the Ouse and along the coast, and keeps handy ships to fetch its food-rents and carry its letters.
ships.picture: A ten-metre ship with one mast drawn up on the strand, a monk and a boatman arguing over her worn planks while a boy bails her.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json. That the minster kept and sold ships is the game's inference from its estates (?)

ships.how: bought on the strand any week, or built in a month
ships.note: The river's own boats: for eels and salmon, for lightering goods up from a hull that cannot reach the bank, for crossing to the old town on the far side.
ships.picture: A tarred open boat with two oars nosing through reeds, eel traps stacked in her bow, the ten-sided tower above the bank.
ships.source: The class from ship_classes_793.json; fish bones in quantity from the York digs (?)

ships.how: built to order by Danish wrights from 876, or bought from a crew that has taken land and means to stay
ships.note: When the army shared out the land its ships lay in the Ouse with nobody to row them. For a generation York is the cheapest place in England to buy a northern hull, and afterwards the best place to have one built.
ships.picture: A long low ship with a carved stem hauled half out of the river, her oar-ports shuttered, a man with a plough-ox looking her over like a horse he no longer needs.
ships.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 876; story/ships_793.json names eoforwic for the later northern classes. Clench nails and reused ship timber from the digs (?)

ships.how: bought from the river people for a few pennies
ships.note: Hollowed trunks work the Foss and the upper Ouse where nothing else floats: reed, eels, firewood.
ships.picture: A man standing in a hollowed log, poling it through flooded willows with a load of cut reed.
ships.source: The class from ship_classes_793.json; logboats are found on the Yorkshire rivers, their dates uncertain (?)

sayings.text: What is a ship? A wandering house, an inn anywhere, a traveller who leaves no track, a neighbour of the sand.
sayings.source: Alcuin of York, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino; own rendering of 'Quid est navis? Domus erratica, ubilibet hospitium, viator sine vestigiis, vicinus harenae' (Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.md) (?)

sayings.text: They became afterwards their harrowers and plowers.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 876 (Ingram 1823), of the army at York; said in the town of any raider who settles down

sayings.text: Both the kings were slain on the spot. The survivors made peace.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 867 (Ingram 1823 (?)), shortened; said at York of any quarrel that two men lost

sayings.text: Three fingers write and the whole body labours. Thank God it grows dark.
sayings.source: A scribe's marginal complaint, of the common kind; own rendering, the second half after the Irish margins (?)

sayings.text: Eight thousand to the bucket, and the bucket is the better buy.
sayings.source: Invented in the period's manner, of the brass stycas; the Hexham hoard held some 8,000 in a bucket (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styca)

sayings.text: A Frank says a Frisian's cloak is too short to cover a lie. At York they say it was long enough to run in.
sayings.source: Invented, turning Notker's story of the short Frisian cloaks (Gesta Karoli I.34, Grant 1907) onto the flight of 773 (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11)

sayings.text: If a merchant fares three times over the wide sea at his own cost, he is worth a thegn's right.
sayings.source: The tract on people's ranks, about 1005, in Archbishop Wulfstan's books; own rendering (Thorpe 1840 has it; Design/content/lore/texts_books.md no. 33). Said from 1002

sayings.text: I will not die lying down, like a cow.
sayings.source: Earl Siward, dying at York in 1055, by Henry of Huntingdon's twelfth-century telling; paraphrased (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siward,_Earl_of_Northumbria). Said from 1055

sayings.text: The world is in haste, and it nears its end. So pay what you owe today.
sayings.source: The first half from Archbishop Wulfstan's Sermon of the Wolf, 1014, own rendering of 'theos worold is on ofste, and hit nealaecth tham ende'; the second half is the ale-house's

easter_eggs.text: Lower a bucket in the old square well and it knocks on something that is not stone. Down in the black water lies a helmet with a boar-nosed face guard and a strip of bright metal over its crown that reads, in Latin: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Spirit of God, and to all the saints, we offer Oshere. Nobody now alive knows who Oshere was or why his helmet was hidden. Leave it: it will lie there a thousand years.
easter_eggs.source: The Coppergate helmet, eighth century, found in a wood-lined well on 12 May 1982: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coppergate_Helmet. Own rendering of the inscription

easter_eggs.text: In the book room one chest has a gap in its list: seven titles crossed through and beside them, in a young hand, 'with the Frisian, in the year of the brawl'. The books are in the school's chest at Traiectum.
easter_eggs.source: Liudger went home about 773 'having with him a store of books': Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.12 (the spine's rendering). The list and the number seven are ours

easter_eggs.text: In the brass years one moneyer, Leofthegn, cuts dies far finer than the metal deserves: a small hound on one, a cross of pellets on another. Ask why and he says a man must look at something all day.
easter_eggs.source: Leofdegn, moneyer under Æthelred II (about 841-849), known for his fancy dies: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styca. The hound is on a real coin of his (?); the remark is ours

easter_eggs.text: A new penny of King Sihtric has a sword on it, a hammer, and a small cross. Ask the moneyer which god it is for and he says: the one who is looking.
easter_eggs.source: Sihtric's coin with 'both Thor's hammer and the cross': Victoria County History, City of York; the Saint Peter pennies with sword and hammer (?). The remark is ours

easter_eggs.text: In the kings' hall, about the year Eric rules, they tell of an Icelander who came to his enemy's hall by mistake, made a praise-poem in one night to buy back his head, and was let go at dawn. The king's men say the poem was good. The king says it was long.
easter_eggs.source: Egil's Head-Ransom at Eric's hall at York, about 948: Egils saga, a thirteenth-century saga and not a record (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Bloodaxe). texts_793.json has verses of it (verse:v01_hofudlausn_west_over_sea). The king's remark is ours

easter_eggs.text: Behind a house in the long plots a man has left, in the pit, the largest proof of a meal of meat and bran bread that anyone will ever find. He had worms. So does everybody.
easter_eggs.source: The 'Lloyds Bank coprolite', ninth century, 20 cm long, from Pavement: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyds_Bank_coprolite

easter_eggs.text: A Dublin man in the ale-house shows a small shell, smooth and spotted, that came from a sea so warm nobody here believes in it, and a silver coin with writing like worm tracks struck at the far end of the world.
easter_eggs.source: A cowrie from the Red Sea or the Persian Gulf and coins from Samarkand, found at York: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_York. A dirham of 903-908 from Coppergate: silver_coin.md

easter_eggs.text: On the way west toward Harrogate a man has turned off the road with a spade and a heavy bag. He is not there when you look again. He never comes back for it.
easter_eggs.source: The Vale of York hoard, buried 927-928: a gilt Frankish cup holding 617 coins, in a lead box (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_York_Hoard); riddles_793.json rw_hoard_vale_of_york

unlocks.gives: flag yk_paid: no host needed at Eoforwic; prices a tenth better; Frisian hulls appear on the strand; Aldger goes ashore; Thiadburg's surety at Dorestad (db_surety)

unlocks.what: guest-friendship with the host's line: a bench, a peg and a tally that outlives its owners
unlocks.how: Lodge with Wulfheard in three different years and leave no debt on the stick; or be shown the old stick by Thorgerd or Sigrid
unlocks.gives: flag guest_friend_eoforwic: lodge and store here without rent; the host witnesses sales for nothing; rumours a week fresher; Thorgerd (from 878) and Sigrid (from 1040) greet the heirs as the house of the old stick

unlocks.how: Sit with Torhthelm in the book room (the card harbour.chain_lindisfarne_book.s03_calves) or bring him good calfskin twice
unlocks.gives: flag bk_knows_worth: books can be priced and sold in any market, heathen or Christian; the riddle of the bookworm (give_riddle riddle_exeter_47_bookworm)

unlocks.how: Pay for the bell-house tin, or carry the chest for Tours, or stand with the church through the army's years
unlocks.gives: sanctuary, lodging and a witness at Saint Peter's for the house and its heirs; the bell rung for the ship in fog; Alcuin's letter (give_text alcuin_793)

unlocks.what: leave to trade both sides of the line between the two armies

unlocks.gives: flag en_hostage_given without giving a hostage of the house's own; no seizure in English ports for carrying York goods, nor at York for carrying southern ones

unlocks.how: From 905, answer the skald's riddles of the giant's kin (riddles_793.json set ymirs_kin) before the king
unlocks.gives: audience and feast at the kings' garth without a gift; the Dublin kin's road over the hills is told (a tip for duiblinn); a verse of the Head-Ransom (give_text verse:v01_hofudlausn_west_over_sea)

unlocks.how: From 900: 350 d and the lawmen's leave (story/unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_eoforwic); at half price if the house sold to the army and stayed; or by the archbishop's gift at the end of the Lindisfarne book chain
unlocks.gives: buy_plot at Eoforwic: a house, a workshop to let, and the right to build the staith; a factor can be kept here (unlock_factor_eoforwic)
